An outbreak in one town reaches the next through the people who travel between them. In Starsim, places are a stratification of the model (a **spatial** one, with each place a level), and movement between them is optional: without it, each place has its own epidemic, and with it, infection passes from place to place. This is the metapopulation model, with each place a subpopulation that mixes within itself and is linked to the others by movement. It works the same under compartments and agents, and its results can be drawn on maps, as [below](#maps). The tutorial [T6 – Geography and mixing](../tutorials/t6_places.qmd) builds up a model of several towns step by step; this page is for looking things up. The data on places that comes with Starsim is on [Population data](populations_data.qmd).

## Towns linked by commuting

A **geography** (`ss.geo.geography`) is a set of named places, with the population of each and where they are. Stratifying a disease by it (`stratify(patch=towns)`) makes a copy of each state for each place, and `mobility=` says how people move between them, given with the places as `stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=...))`. Here are three towns of measles: Riverton, with 60,000 people, Hillside (30,000) 20 km away, and Lakeside (10,000) 50 km away, with 10 infectious people in Riverton at the start. People spend 0.1% of their time in the other towns, split between them by a gravity model (more to bigger and nearer towns):

```{python}
import starsim as ss

towns = ss.geo.geography(
    names       = ['Riverton', 'Hillside', 'Lakeside'],
    populations = [60_000, 30_000, 10_000],
    x           = [0, 20, 50], # Positions in km
    y           = [0, 0, 10],
)

S, R = ss.states('S R')
I = ss.State('I', infected=True) # Infected: counted in the results infected and prevalence
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0]))) # 10 infectious people in Riverton
measles.stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.001)))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, stop=ss.days(60))
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.by('patch').plot()
```

The sim takes its population (100,000) from the geography. Each town has its own epidemic, a few days after the one before: Hillside, which is bigger and nearer, before Lakeside. Without `mobility=`, people mix only within their own town, and the outbreak stays in Riverton:

```{python}
isolated = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0])), name='measles')
isolated.stratify(patch=towns) # The same towns, with no movement between them

no_movement = ss.Sim(isolated, stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0)
no_movement.run()
print('Infections with movement:')
print(sim.results.measles.infection.by('patch').summarize().round())
print('Infections without movement:')
print(no_movement.results.measles.infection.by('patch').summarize().round())
```

Even 0.1% of people's time spent away is enough to carry measles, with an R0 of 15, to every town; a disease with a lower R0 needs more movement to spread, and arrives later.

## Geographies

A geography can be given by hand, read from a file, or looked up by country:

```python
ss.geo.geography(names=['a', 'b'], populations=[10_000, 20_000], x=[0, 30], y=[0, 0])  # Positions in any unit of distance
ss.geo.geography(names=['a', 'b'], populations=[10_000, 20_000], lat=[-1.3, -0.1], lon=[36.8, 34.8]) # Latitudes and longitudes; distances in km
ss.geo.geography(names=['a', 'b'], populations=[10_000, 20_000], distances=[[0, 30], [30, 0]])   # Distances directly
ss.geo.geography('districts.csv')               # A table with columns name, pop, and x and y (or lat and lon)
ss.geo.geography('districts.shp')               # Shapes (.shp, .geojson, or .gpkg, read with geopandas); each place at the center of its shape
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)              # Kenya's 47 counties, with populations and positions
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1, places=['Nairobi', 'Kiambu']) # Some of them
ss.geo.geography(['Kenya', 'Uganda'], level=1)  # Several countries, with places named e.g. 'Kenya:Busia'
ss.geo.geography(['Kenya', 'Uganda', 'Tanzania'], level=0) # Each country as one place
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=2)              # The units below the counties (downloaded the first time)
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1, year=2010)   # The counties' populations in another year (downloaded the first time)
```

A country's administrative units come from `starsim_data`: level 0 is the country itself, level 1 its counties, provinces, or states, and level 2 the units below them. Levels 0 and 1 are bundled for 184 countries and territories, so they need no download; level 2, and populations for a year other than 2020, are downloaded the first time (level 2 needs the optional package geopandas: `pip install starsim_data[spatial]`). The places that have units, and how many, are listed on [Population data](populations_data.qmd#appendix-every-place-and-its-data). Each unit comes with its population, position, area (`kenya.area`, in km²), and p-code (`kenya.codes`, e.g. `'KE047'` for Nairobi), the standard code of an administrative unit, which is the reliable way to join surveillance data reported by unit to the places of a model, since names are spelled in different ways.

Here measles starts in Nairobi and spreads across Kenya's counties, in a population that is 90% immune (as from vaccination), so that R0 = 15 gives an effective reproduction number of about 1.5:

```{python}
kenya = ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)

measles_kenya = ss.Disease(infection, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=0.9),                         # 90% immune at the start
    init_n = dict(I=ss.by(patch={'Nairobi': 10})), # 10 infectious people in Nairobi, and none in the other 46 counties
)
measles_kenya.stratify(patch=ss.levels(kenya, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.001)))

sim = ss.Sim(measles_kenya, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles_kenya
for county in ['Nairobi', 'Kiambu', 'Mombasa', 'Turkana']:
    peak = res.I.select(patch=county).values.argmax()
    print(county, '- infectious people peak on', res.timevec[peak])
```

Kiambu borders Nairobi, Mombasa is the second city, 440 km away, and Turkana is a remote county in the northwest. Nairobi's outbreak peaks first, in June; Kiambu's follows in July, and Mombasa's and Turkana's in September, near the peaks of most other counties. The gravity model sends Nairobi's travelers to every county, near or far, in proportion to its population, so distance matters less than it might: Turkana, remote as it is, peaks within days of Mombasa. As an ODE, a county's outbreak starts as soon as the first fraction of an infected person arrives (see [below](#under-compartments-and-agents) for why agents differ).

A geography with no populations (`names=` only) gives places of equal size. A place's population sets the share of people who start there.

## Maps

A result of a model stratified by place can be drawn on a map of the places, with the result's `map()`. Each place is colored by the result there, and drawn as its shape, if the geography has shapes, or else as a point at its position, with an area in proportion to its population. Since places differ in size, a share, such as the prevalence, usually shows the spread better than a count. `shapes=True` draws a country's units as their boundaries, which are downloaded the first time (this needs geopandas: `pip install starsim_data[spatial]`). Here is the outbreak above, on the first of May, July, and September:

```{python}
res.prevalence.map(t=['2025-05-01', '2025-07-01', '2025-09-01'], shapes=True)
```

In May, the outbreak is in Nairobi alone; by July it has spread to the counties around it, and by September, when it is over in Nairobi, it is at its height across the rest of the country. The options:

| Call | What it draws |
|---|---|
| `res.map()` | One map of the result's summary in each place over the run, as `summarize()` gives it (the total of a flow, the mean of a ratio, the final value of a stock) |
| `res.map(n=6)` | Six maps, evenly spaced from the start of the outbreak to its end |
| `res.map(t='2025-02-01')` | The map on one date, or on each of a list of dates (or times, e.g. `t=[15, 25]`, for a sim without dates) |
| `res.map(animate=True)` | An animation, shown in a notebook with controls to play it; elsewhere, it is returned as a Matplotlib animation |
| `res.map(animate=True, filename='spread.gif')` | The same, saved to a file (a GIF, or an MP4, which needs ffmpeg) |
| `res.map(shapes=True)` | For a country, its units' boundaries, downloaded the first time (this needs geopandas: `pip install starsim_data[spatial]`); a geography read from shapes always draws them |
| `geo.plot()` | The places of a geography, with their populations |
| `geo.plot(values=..., label=...)` | The places colored by a value for each one, in order or by name, e.g. a summary of a result: `kenya.plot(values=res.infection.by('patch').summarize()/kenya.populations, label='Share infected')` |

Both take `cmap=` (the colors, by default from white to red), `vmin=` and `vmax=` (the range of the color scale), and `names=` (whether to label the places, by default when there are 15 or fewer). A result of agents is mapped the same way; for the runs of a MultiSim, map one run (`res.select(run=0)`).

## Movement

Movement has three parts: its shape (which places people go to), its amount (how much they go), and its kind (what moving means).

**The shape** comes from a movement model or a matrix:

- `ss.geo.gravity(source_power=1, dest_power=1, distance_power=2)`: the movement from place *i* to place *j* is proportional to *pop*~i~^*s*−1^ × *pop*~j~^*d*^ / *distance*~ij~^*r*^ (with *s*, *d*, and *r* its `source_power`, `dest_power`, and `distance_power`), so people go more to bigger and nearer places.
- `ss.geo.radiation()`: the radiation model (Simini et al. 2012), which has no parameters to fit: of the people who travel from a place, the share who go to each other one depends on the populations of the places nearer to it.
- `ss.geo.Mobility(matrix=M)`: a matrix that you already have, with the movement from each place (rows) to each place (columns), e.g. from commuting data. For many places, a SciPy sparse array keeps only the pairs that share anyone.
- `ss.geo.Mobility(matrix=kenya.adjacency)`: movement only between places that share a border, split evenly between each place's neighbors (`adjacency` is true for each pair of units that share a border, and is there for a country's units at level 1, or given to `ss.geo.geography(adjacency=...)`). This is the classic model of spread from district to district.

**The amount** is `away=`, the share of their time that people spend away from home, split between the other places by the shape. With neither `away=` nor `scale=`, it is 10%, which `describe()` marks as guessed. `scale=` instead gives the amount as a constant in the gravity formula; its units depend on the powers, so no value fits both three towns and a country, and it is for an amount that has been fitted to data.

**The kind** is given with `kind=`, on the movement model or the matrix (`ss.geo.gravity(kind='visit')`, `ss.geo.Mobility(M, kind='migrate')`); by default it is commuting. The kinds are different mechanisms, and the numbers of a matrix mean different things under each (a share of time, or a rate of moving home), so changing the kind without changing the numbers does not give an equivalent model:

| Kind | What it means | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `'commute'` (default) | People keep their home, and spend a share of their time in other places, where they can be infected and infect others | Daily travel to work, school, and markets |
| `'visit'` | As for commuting, but visitors can only be infected away from home, and infect nobody there | Short trips; flepiMoP's form |
| `'migrate'` | People move home, at the rates the movement gives (per person per unit time) | Migration and relocation; needs `scale=` as the rate |
| `'force'` | Nobody moves; a share of each place's force of infection goes to the others | LASER's form |

Under commuting, with *T*~ik~ the share of their time that people from place *i* spend in place *k* (so each row of *T* sums to 1), the force of infection on people from place *i* is

$$\lambda_i = \sum_k T_{ik} \, \beta \, \frac{\sum_j T_{jk} I_j}{\sum_j T_{jk} N_j}$$

the standard time-share form: people are exposed in each place in proportion to the time they spend there, to whoever is there. It needs no change to the time step, and does not follow the time of day.

```python
ss.geo.gravity(away=0.2)                    # Commuting, 20% of time away
ss.geo.gravity(away=0.2, kind='visit')      # Visiting
ss.geo.gravity(scale=2e-5, kind='migrate')  # Migration, at rates from the gravity model
ss.geo.radiation(away=0.1, kind='force')    # A moving force of infection, as in LASER
```

### Movement between neighbors

With movement only across borders, infection spreads as a wave, from each county to its neighbors, rather than from Nairobi to everywhere at once. Here is the Kenya model above, with the same amount of movement, but only between counties that share a border:

```{python}
measles_borders = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch={'Nairobi': 10})))
measles_borders.stratify(patch=ss.levels(kenya, mobility=ss.geo.Mobility(matrix=kenya.adjacency, away=0.001)))

borders = ss.Sim(measles_borders, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)
borders.run()
res_borders = borders.results.measles_borders
for county in ['Nairobi', 'Kiambu', 'Mombasa', 'Turkana']:
    share = res_borders.infection.select(patch=county).values.sum()/kenya.populations[kenya.names.index(county)]
    print(county, '- share infected in 2025:', round(share, 3))
res_borders.prevalence.map(t=['2025-07-01', '2025-09-01', '2025-11-01'], shapes=True)
```

The outbreak in Nairobi is the same, but it now reaches only the counties next to it, and then theirs: by the end of the year, it is still growing in Mombasa, on the coast, and has barely begun in Turkana, in the far northwest: 1.4% and 0.4% of their people are infected in the year, against 6% in each with movement by gravity. Which shape fits a setting is a question for data on travel, such as surveys, mobile phone data, or the timing of past outbreaks in each place.

### A movement register

A table of moves on given dates (a movement register, such as livestock sales between farms) is `ss.geo.register(...)`, a file name or a DataFrame with columns `date`, `from`, `to`, and `n`, and optionally `states`. Each row moves `n` people from one place to another on that date: a row with no `from` adds people (births, purchases), and one with no `to` removes them (deaths, sales out of the model). The people who move are chosen at random from those in `states` (by default, everyone), and people added go into the first state, unless `states` says otherwise. Here 100 people move from Riverton to Lakeside on day 5, while measles is spreading there, and 50 people (all susceptible) join Hillside, which has no other link to Riverton:

```{python}
import pandas as pd

register = pd.DataFrame({
    'date': [5, 5],
    'from': ['Riverton', None],
    'to':   ['Lakeside', 'Hillside'],
    'n':    [100, 50],
})
measles_moves = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0])))
measles_moves.stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=ss.geo.register(register)))

sim = ss.Sim(measles_moves, stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles_moves.infection.by('patch').plot()
```

Lakeside's outbreak starts with the infectious people among those who moved; Hillside has none.

## Values by place

Anything that can vary by level of a stratification can vary by place, with `ss.by(patch=...)`: a value for each place, in order, or a dict by name. Above, `init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0]))` starts the outbreak in one place, as does `ss.by(patch={'Riverton': 10})`: in a starting value (`init`, `init_n`, or `init_prev`), a place left out of a dict starts with 0, while a rate or other parameter by name needs every place, since a missing one there is more likely a mistake; a transmission rate by place is `S >> I @ ss.by(patch=[1.9, 1.9, 1.0])*I`. Results are by place too: `by('patch')` splits a result into one column for each place, and `select()` picks one, e.g. `sim.results.measles.I.select(patch='Hillside')`. Contact matrices act within each place, so a model can be stratified by age and by place together, with a contact matrix by age (see [Population data](populations_data.qmd)).

The amount of movement can be fitted to data like any other parameter, by giving it bounds: `ss.geo.gravity(away=ss.par(0.01, bounds=[0.001, 0.1]))` (see [Fitting a model](calibration_fitting.qmd)).

## Under compartments and agents

Places and movement work the same under every solver: with agents, each agent has a home place, and commuting and visiting weight its exposure by where it spends its time. Where they differ is in how infection first reaches a place. In an ODE, a tiny fraction of an infected person in a town starts its epidemic growing at once; with agents, a whole person there has to be infected first, which takes longer, and by chance may not happen at all. With less movement than above, the difference is large:

```{python}
measles_slow = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0])))
measles_slow.stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.0001)))

kw = dict(stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0)
for label, sim in {'As an ODE': ss.Sim(measles_slow, **kw), 'As agents': ss.Sim(measles_slow, n_agents=10_000, **kw)}.items():
    sim.run()
    peaks = sim.results.measles_slow.I.by('patch').values.argmax(axis=0)
    print(label, '- day of the peak in Riverton, Hillside, and Lakeside:', peaks)
```

As an ODE, Hillside and Lakeside peak 3 or 4 days after Riverton; as agents, 7 and 13 days after. (Riverton itself peaks later as agents too, for reasons that have nothing to do with places: its outbreak starts from one agent, who stands for the 10 infectious people, and agents take steps of a day, which is long for measles; see [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd).) For questions about whether, or when, an outbreak reaches a small place, agents (or a stochastic compartmental model: see [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd)) give the better answer; for the size of an epidemic across places that are all well seeded, an ODE is enough.

## Pitfalls

- **A name does not make a place.** A stratification is spatial when it is given a geography (`patch=towns`) or `kind='space'` (`stratify(patch=ss.levels(['a', 'b'], kind='space'))`). A list of names alone, even `patch=['north', 'south']`, makes ordinary groups, whose people mix with each other; a stratification named like places (`patch`, `region`, `district`, `county`, `province`, `place`, or `location`) given only names says so in a note, unless `kind=` is given. `describe()` gives the kind of each stratification: `patch (space)` or `patch (plain)`.

- **A movement model needs a geography.** `ss.geo.gravity()` and `ss.geo.radiation()` work out the movement from the places' populations and distances, so on a stratification with no geography they raise an error; give a geography, or the movement itself as a matrix.
- **Too much movement.** With `scale=` instead of `away=`, the gravity formula can send people from a small place to a large one for more than all of their time; Starsim then caps it at all of it, with a warning. Give `away=` unless `k` has been fitted.
- **Start the outbreak somewhere.** `init_prev=0.01` infects 1% of people in every place; to start it in one place, give `init_n` (or `init`) by place, e.g. `init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch={'Nairobi': 10}))`.
- **Check the links.** Before trusting a spatial model, seed one place and check that the others stay free of infection with no movement (as above), and that with migration, the population of each place changes as it should. With agents that each stand for several people, the number of people who move and the number of agents who move are not the same.
- **Strata multiply.** Every place multiplies the number of compartments: 47 counties × 16 age groups × 3 states is 2,256 compartments. An ODE handles that easily, but results by group take memory, and a model can grow large by accident; `describe()` lists each stratification with its levels.

The API reference for this page: [ss.geo](../api/geo.qmd).

## Further reading

- [LASER: Migration](https://laser.idmod.org/laser-generic/software-overview/migration/): movement between places in an agent-based model, with gravity and radiation models
- [flepiMoP: Model description](https://iddynamics.gitbook.io/flepimop/gempyor/model-description): metapopulation models of US states and counties, with mobility between them
- [MEmilio: Metapopulation models](https://memilio.readthedocs.io/en/latest/cpp/metapop.html): compartmental models of regions joined by commuting
- [Simini et al. 2012: A universal model for mobility and migration patterns](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10856): the radiation model

## Appendix: what a geography has

The attributes of a geography (`kenya = ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)`), for making maps, movement matrices of your own, or joining data by place:

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `names` | The name of each place, in order: the levels of the stratification |
| `populations` | The population of each place (None if not given) |
| `lat`, `lon` | The latitude and longitude of each place, in degrees (for a country's units, the center of each unit) |
| `x`, `y` | The positions of the places, for a geography given by hand with `x=` and `y=` |
| `distances` | The distance between each pair of places (in km, from latitudes and longitudes) |
| `adjacency` | Whether each pair of places shares a border (for a country's units at level 1 or below, or as given) |
| `area` | The area of each place, in km² (for a country's units) |
| `codes` | The p-code of each place (for a country's units), e.g. `'KE047'` |
| `shapes` | The shapes of the places, for a geography read from shapes (None otherwise; `res.map(shapes=True)` downloads a country's) |
| `ref` | Where a country's units came from, which `describe()` shows |

`len(kenya)` is the number of places, and `kenya.plot()` draws them (see [Maps](#maps)).
